title: 道德經 第三十六章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 36, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 70. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 36 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 微明 (The Fine Light). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
將欲歙之，
必固張之；
將欲弱之，
必固強之；
將欲廢之，
必固興之；
將欲奪之，
必固與之。
是謂微明。

morph.gloss: about to, on the point of — an adverb standing before the verb
to want to, to set out to
to draw in, to close up — the breath pulled back in, a thing gathered shut
it — the object pronoun, with no antecedent anywhere: the text does not say what
first, in the first place (固 in its sense 'assuredly'); many editors read the graph as standing for 姑 gū, 'for the time being'
to stretch out, to draw a bow open, to spread wide
weak — used causatively here, with 之 after it: to make weak
strong — causative: to make strong (qiáng; qiǎng would be 'to force')
to scrap, to let fall into disuse — causative: to do away with
to raise up, to set flourishing (xīng)
to seize, to take away by force
to give (yǔ); read yù it would mean 'to take part in'
the fine light — sight of what is still too faint to be seen
too fine to lay hold of: minute, faint, imperceptible

sentences.i: What you would draw in, you must first stretch out; what you would weaken, you must first make strong; what you would do away with, you must first raise up; what you would take away, you must first give. This is called the fine light.
sentences.n: Four couplets on one pattern — 將欲 X 之，必固 Y 之, 'on the point of X-ing it, one must first Y it' — and two grammar lessons inside it. 弱 and 強 are the ordinary adjectives 'weak' and 'strong', but with 之 after them they are verbs that make a thing weak or strong; nothing on the page marks the change, and the next unit brings the same two characters straight back as adjectives. And 之 is the object pronoun eight times over with nothing to refer to: the text never says what is being drawn in, and does not need to. 固 is the disputed word. Read as 'assuredly, in the first place' it gives what stands here; read as standing for 姑 gū, 'for the time being', it sharpens the whole passage into advice from a schemer — stretch him now so as to fold him later. That is how the passage was heard early, and it is the one place in the book that makes readers uneasy. Wang Bi hears it the other way round: this is how hard and violent things undo themselves, the ruler needing only to go along with each thing's own nature and let it destroy itself, which is why the closing line calls the knowledge a light and not a trick. 微明 is bound as one word because the text christens it outright — 是謂, 'this is called' — and a phrase the text names is a word to be learned whole; chapter 27's 襲明, the carried-on light, was bound for the same reason.

sentences.t:
柔弱勝剛強。
魚不可脫於淵，
國之利器不可以示人。

morph.gloss: the soft and yielding — a standing pair in this book, and here a noun, the party that wins
to overcome, to get the better of
the hard and strong — the opposing pair
may, is permitted to — 不可 here forbids rather than reports an inability: the fish must not do it
to slip out of, to get clear of
from, out of — the all-purpose preposition, standing after its verb
a deep pool, the still abyss of water
a state, a ruler's domain — a walled capital and the land it holds
the sharp instrument — a state's weapons and engines of power; Wang Bi takes 利 as a verb and reads 'the instruments by which a state is benefited'
sharp, keen-edged; to benefit, to do good to
a vessel, an implement — anything shaped so as to be used
may — 不可以示人, they must not be shown to people
by them — the means, with the object left out
to show, to put on display

sentences.l:
The soft and weak overcome the hard and strong.
A fish must not slip out of the deep pool,
and a state's sharp instruments must not be shown to men.
sentences.i: The soft and yielding overcome the hard and strong. A fish must not leave the deep, and the sharp instruments of a state must not be put on show.
sentences.n: The first line brings back two of the verbs of the unit before, standing still: 弱 and 強, which were 'make weak' and 'make strong' there, are bare qualities here, and each has taken a partner — 柔 and 剛 — to make one of the two standing terms this book turns on. 可 is the character to be careful with. It does not make what follows passive as a rule: in 道可道, the book's first line, the thing spoken of was already the subject, so English came out passive. Here the fish is the one doing the slipping, and 不可 forbids rather than reports an inability — the fish must not leave the deep. Wang Bi is explicit: 魚脫於淵，則必見失矣, 'let the fish slip out of the deep and it is certainly lost.' Notice too 以 with nothing after it in 不可以示人: the means is the instruments just named and is simply dropped, as in chapter 30. What the fish is doing beside the weapons is old and unsettled. The likeliest reading is that both are things that last only while unseen — out of the deep the fish is finished, and a state's instruments once displayed are a state's instruments spent. Wang Bi makes it a lesson in government: 利器, he says, are the implements that benefit the state, and to show them to men is to fall back on punishments; let the ruler go by the nature of things and take no hold, and the implements are never seen while everything finds its place.
